newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed hits out at Russian budget.
newsitem.headline: Lebed hits out at Russian budget.

text.p: Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed, fresh from making peace in Chechnya, has turned his attention to the budget and demanded the government radically overhaul its plans for next year, a newspaper said on Friday.

"General Launches Attack on Budget," the liberal daily Izvestia said in a front-page headline over extracts of a letter it said the 46-year-old former paratroop general had sent to President Boris Yeltsin criticising government spending plans.
It said Lebed's office confirmed the letter was sent to the president, who is resting ahead of heart surgery, on August 29. A similar letter was sent to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
It attacks what it says is the underfunding of the military and sectors ranging from agriculture to industry, high technology, science, culture and education.

The remedy, says Lebed, is for new revenue to be raised by raising prices for natural resources, ending foreign firms' preferential import duties, putting export duties on gas and charging higher rents for the use of state property.

"We suggest that it is advisable to charge the government of the Russian Federation to substantially revise its forecast and the 1997 budget bill, with a view to making provision for decisions on the main goals and tasks of economic development and meeting the demands of national security," he wrote.

Lebed is secretary of the presidential Security Council and not a member of Chernomyrdin's government. He makes no secret of his own presidential ambitions and, during Yeltsin's recent absence, speculation has been rife of a power struggle in the Kremlin involving Lebed and Chernomyrdin, among others.
When he took office last June, he said he would deal with not only defence and internal security but also with "economic security" and the fight against organised crime and corruption.
He has mostly been busy in the past weeks with reaching a peace agreement with Chechen separatist rebels.
Despite a nationalistic outlook and insistence on strong centralised government, Lebed has espoused a free market.

But one of his aides in the Security Council apparatus, Sergei Glazyev, favours a stronger state role in the economy. He has accused ministers of drawing up a budget to favour certain vested interests rather than the whole nation.

Lebed arrived in Minsk on Friday for talks with Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, Itar-Tass news agency said. Among other topics of discussion would be the setting up of a common air defence system.
